name: Rejection of purpose: chance and necessity
plain_explanation: Empedocles believed the changes in the world are not directed toward any goal or purpose; they happen simply because of Chance and Necessity acting on the elements, moved by Love and Strife.
precise_definition: Empedocles' doctrine that cosmic change is governed 'not by any purpose, but only by Chance and Necessity,' including a crude evolutionary account in which countless random combinations of body parts arose and only certain viable forms survived.
why_it_mattered: Russell singles this out as making Empedocles 'more scientific' than Parmenides, Plato, and Aristotle in this particular respect, prefiguring later mechanistic (rather than teleological) explanations of nature, including the atomists' fully mechanistic cosmology in the following chapters.
historical_origin: Part of Empedocles' cosmological and biological speculation, including his fantastic proto-evolutionary account of early monstrous life-forms.
examples: Early 'countless tribes of mortal creatures... with all manner of forms': heads without necks, solitary limbs seeking union, hybrid ox-human creatures
Only certain combinations proving viable and surviving, an early anticipation of survival of the fittest
competing_positions: Anaxagoras's introduction of Mind (nous) as a directing cause (treated in the next chapter), and the general teleological tendency of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates, however fantastically, the later Darwinian idea of natural selection acting on random variation.
